The central question is whether attention sinks — those fixed anchor positions (typically token 0 and a handful of early tokens) that absorb disproportionate attention mass regardless of semantic content — are merely a symptom of context degradation beyond pretraining sequence length, or whether they actively cause it by monopolizing attention capacity that should route to genuinely informative tokens. The key concepts are: positional bias in softmax attention (the sink emerges because softmax must sum to 1 and needs somewhere to "dump" weight when no token is contextually relevant), RoPE's extrapolation failure (at positions beyond the training horizon, positional encodings become geometrically incoherent, amplifying sink attraction), and the distinction between perplexity degradation and retrieval/reasoning degradation (a model can still predict next tokens tolerably while catastrophically failing to surface information from far-earlier context). A subtler concern is that mitigation strategies like StreamingLLM (which preserves sink tokens explicitly) treat the symptom by stabilizing softmax normalization, but do nothing to recover the lost routing capacity — the heads that perpetually fire on sinks during long-context inference are heads that are not attending to your 8,000-token-ago passage, and no amount of sink preservation restores that signal.

The implication is a specific failure cascade: early-layer sink heads suppress the positional signal needed to correctly route token representations into middle-layer binding computations, so by the time activations reach the layers that would perform retrieval or coreference, the positional scaffolding has already been corrupted — the middle layers are trying to bind entities whose positional context was never cleanly encoded. Late layers appear relatively protected because their attention is more content-addressed and less positionally anchored, which is why models can still generate fluent, locally coherent text at extreme context lengths while simultaneously failing catastrophically on needle-in-a-haystack retrieval tasks — the late-layer fluency machinery remains functional while the mid-layer retrieval machinery has collapsed. The distinction matters enormously and the residual stream geometry points toward corrupted signal rather than absent signal — specifically, middle layers under sink-driven capacity loss are still writing to the residual stream, but they are writing positionally incoherent entity bindings: the MLP and attention outputs at layers 8–16 add vectors that encode "entity X is at position P" where P is systematically wrong or underspecified because the positional scaffolding was corrupted in early layers, and this corrupted write is harder for late layers to correct than a zero vector would be, because it actively misleads the residual stream's directional geometry. Elhage et al.'s (2021) residual stream superposition framework predicts exactly this failure mode: when a feature (entity-position binding) is written with the wrong coefficient into a shared superposition basis, downstream layers reading that basis dimension receive a signal that is not zero but is anti-correlated with the correct answer — late layers fine-tuned on long contexts must then learn not just to fill a gap but to suppress an actively wrong direction in activation space, which is a harder optimization target and explains why long-context fine-tuning requires disproportionately many gradient steps relative to the apparent task difficulty. Anthropic's residual stream analyses (in the context of superposition and privileged basis work) suggest that late layers in well-trained models develop what amount to "veto" circuits — attention heads whose primary function is to read and null out specific corrupted directions before MLP layers perform factual retrieval — and the hypothesis is that long-context fine-tuning is largely growing these veto circuits rather than fixing upstream corruption. The "parametric memory filling" hypothesis (late layers just hallucinate from weights when context signal is absent) would predict that errors at long context are systematically coherent — plausible-sounding but wrong entity attributions drawn from training distribution statistics — and this is indeed the observed failure mode in NIAH (Needle-in-a-Haystack) benchmarks where models at 32K+ tokens frequently produce confident wrong answers that are contextually plausible rather than incoherent, suggesting parametric memory is being substituted for genuine retrieval. The capacity tax hypothesis is well-supported by indirect evidence: Wang et al.'s (2022) IOI (Indirect Object Identification) circuit analysis in GPT-2 established that late-layer name mover heads are among the most functionally specialized and capacity-constrained components in the network, and these are precisely the heads most likely to be recruited for suppression tasks because they already have machinery for reading entity-position bindings from the residual stream — repurposing them for vetoing corrupted bindings would directly cannibalize the compositional reasoning budget. The clearest detection strategy is behavioral double dissociation: evaluate a base model versus its long-context fine-tuned counterpart on (a) a long-context retrieval task (NIAH at 32K) and (b) a short-context multi-step compositional reasoning task (something like bAbI task 16 or the harder ARC-Challenge subsets) — if fine-tuning improves (a) while measurably degrading (b) on inputs well within the original pretraining context window, you have evidence of compositional capacity cannibalization, and anecdotally practitioners report exactly this regression but it is rarely measured systematically. Mechanistically, the smoking gun would be attention head knockout experiments comparing functional head assignments pre- and post-fine-tuning: if heads that pre-fine-tuning were classified as "S-inhibition" or "name mover" heads (in the IOI taxonomy) post-fine-tuning show altered attention patterns on short-context compositional tasks — attending more to early anchor positions rather than semantically relevant tokens — that confirms repurposing rather than net head growth. The MLP side of this tax is arguably more severe but less studied: late-layer MLPs in transformer LMs function as key-value factual memories (Geva et al., 2021), and if fine-tuning on long contexts increases the frequency with which these MLPs are called upon to substitute parametric memory for failed retrieval, their effective capacity for novel compositional generalization decreases because the same weight matrices are being pulled toward retrieval-substitution behavior. This implies a specific diagnostic: if you plot sink mass versus context length and observe a flat or declining trend up to some threshold followed by a sharp inflection, that inflection point is a more honest estimate of the model's true effective context length than any perplexity-based measure, and the steepness of the inflection predicts how catastrophically retrieval will fail just beyond that threshold.
